The linking subsystem needs attention and should probably be on the roadmap, including around adverse interactions between what's discussed here and the new module system. Without getting into detail what I've concluded is that precompiled modules -- as a workaround to such performance issues --will not work, and there are simply no work-arounds, at least if you're working on a Mac. The Clang compiler packaged with Elan produces object code that won't link with up-to-date Mac libraries; and the obvious workaround of using the native Mac Clang compiler will not work either, because, wait for it, ..., the number of mathlib files that need to be linked into a shared library exceeds the 1MB command line length of Mac's compiler, and there's simply no work-around. Passing the command line parameters in a file doesn't work, maybe due to the 1MB limit reflecting some internal buffer max size. In any case that doesn't work. And tricks like using symbolic links to reduce file names and command line length also fails, as Lean appears to expand symbolically linked file names into full physical paths anyway.

The second disruptive problem we're having is that we've modularized our project into separate packages, and I at least haven't found a practical way (please advise, as I may well have missed something here) to not replicate mathlib for each packages. So we're talking 7+GB * number-of-packages, which for us is up to a dozen or so. Changing a few lines of code near a "root" package can trigger downstream rebuilds that take a huge amount of time -- many hours on one of my student's machines.

Lean 4 is an incredible achievement and its future looks even better, but it's still showing its legacy as a researchy project. I'm very optimistic for its future, but these struggles with the size, build processes, and other issues around presumably any large effort (particularly mathlib) are near-blockers for normal things software engineers need when working on singificant systems.
(Was this posted to the wrong thread @Kevin Sullivan ?)

Maybe! Can you perhaps suggest a better one? (Or I can just delete it. But figured this was about build performance in presence of large projects, particularly mathlib, as so much depends upon it. Sorry if my input was misplaced.)
I think you can just open a new thread under ecosystem infrastructure?

Compiling Lean that uses mathlib, or that seeks to produce a shared .a for mathlib, does not work on a Mac. The Clang compilation system packaged with Elan produces object code that won't link with modern Mac libraries. The standard workaround of using the native Mac Clang compiler does not work because the number of mathlib files that need to be linked into a shared library exceeds the 1MB command line length of the Mac's Clang linker. Passing the command line parameters in a file doesn't work, maybe due to the 1MB limit reflecting some Clang-internal buffer max size. And using symbolic links to reduce file name then command line length also fails, as Lean appears to expand the symbolically linked file names into full physical paths before being passed to the linker.

Do I understand correctly that you have several packages using the same version of mathlib and you wish to share the storage space? If so that is going to be a solved problem in the near term future.

Thank you. It's not exactly precompiledModules=true for mathlib. I was
trying to produce precompiled modules and/or native executables for our
packages, each of which in turn uses mathlib. So for each package we need
linking of our files along with all the mathlib files. That's where the
problem is: the command line to link it all exceeds the max length for
clang on MacOS. Ok, and thank you for the news about a forthcoming fix for
the shared mathlib fix. We're currently standardized on 4.27.0 pending
migration, probably to 4.29.0 when it's ready, so we're set up for this fix.

It doesn't happen often that people want significant parts of Mathlib in their executables. Could you say more about the shape of your Mathlib dependencies, what's the parts that you actually want to be available for native execution in the end?

I think

fix: use response files on all platforms to avoid ARG_MAX lean#12540

is relevant here. Unfortunately now that I've added the lake-ci label, it is failing some of the additional lake tests.

Thank you for this. I'm not sure how to determine my exact mathlib
dependencies, direct and indirect. --Kevin

Response files don't appear to work on MacOS at least. I haven't tested on
Windows. Everything is fine when running in a Linux container until one
needs native compilation and linking. I tried every workaround I (or my
robot, TBH) could come up with. Nothing worked. The same length constraint
kicked in when using response files as when providing all the args directly
on the cmd line. Thank you for your reply. Also maybe #12540 wasn't the
issue you meant to link to. That one's about moving theorems about lists to
batteries. Very best, --Kevin
